faqs.question: So what exactly counts as a virtual proposal card?
faqs.answer: It is a personalised 'will you marry me' card built online and delivered over the internet instead of on paper. It comes either as a file you send — an image, PDF or short video — or as a link that opens into a hosted page with your names, photos and a Yes button.

faqs.question: Should I send a proposal card as an image or as a link?
faqs.answer: Send the link if you want music, a countdown or a reply button, and send an image if you want something that cannot break. The safest version is both: share the link for the moment, then screenshot the page and send that as the keepsake.

faqs.question: Is a virtual proposal card free?
faqs.answer: Most builders let you create and share one at no cost, including SubhSandesh. Paid tiers usually buy custom domains, watermark removal or extra storage rather than a better card.

faqs.question: Will the link still work in a few years?
faqs.answer: Only while the host keeps it online. Pew Research Center found in May 2024 that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were gone a decade later, and 9% of sampled pages were unreachable because the whole root domain had failed. Save a screenshot.

faqs.question: Can they actually say no on a virtual proposal card?
faqs.answer: On most builders the No button dodges the cursor or shrinks, so technically no. That is a joke, not a safeguard — if the answer is genuinely uncertain, ask in person and send the card afterwards.

faqs.question: How do I send a virtual proposal card on WhatsApp?
faqs.answer: Copy the page link and paste it into the chat, or attach the exported image directly. Expect it to be opened on a phone: 48.9% of the 51,164 views recorded across SubhSandesh pages happen on phones, and 49.1% on a touch device of some kind.

faqs.question: Can I password-protect a virtual proposal card?
faqs.answer: Yes, on any builder that hosts the card as a page rather than handing you a file. Across all 4,524 pages created on SubhSandesh since March 2026, 40.0% were password-locked by their creator before sharing — a platform-wide rate, not a proposal-specific one.

faqs.question: Does a virtual proposal card work without internet?
faqs.answer: A downloaded image or video does, because it lives in the phone's gallery. A hosted link does not — it needs a connection every single time it is opened, which matters if the recipient has patchy data.

faqs.question: Is a virtual proposal card a real proposal?
faqs.answer: It is a real way to ask, and for a long-distance couple it is often the only one available. For a proposal happening in the same room it is usually a worse object than paper, and the card works better as the thing you send afterwards.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a virtual proposal card and a bridesmaid proposal card?
faqs.answer: A bridesmaid proposal card asks someone to be in your wedding party; a virtual proposal card asks someone to marry you. Search results for the phrase mix the two heavily, so check what a template is actually for before editing it.

faqs.question: Can I print a virtual proposal card?
faqs.answer: Only if it is a file. An image or PDF prints at any photo shop for a few rupees; a hosted page can only be screenshotted, which loses the music, the countdown and the button along with it.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Virtual Proposal Card: A File You Send or a Link That Opens

A virtual proposal card is a marriage proposal delivered digitally, and it arrives in one of two shapes: a **file** you download and send — an image, a PDF, a short video — or a **link** that opens into a hosted page. That single choice decides everything else. A file survives a screenshot, needs no signal to reopen and sits in their gallery for years; a link can play a song, run a countdown and record the answer, but it lives only as long as somebody keeps paying for the server. On SubhSandesh, 40.0% of creators password-protect a page before sharing it — that is a platform-wide figure across all 4,524 pages created since 12 March 2026, not a proposal-specific one — and 48.9% of the 51,164 recorded views happen on a phone. Below: the three formats, what each can genuinely do, and the tradeoff in both directions.

## What is a virtual proposal card?

A virtual proposal card is a personalised "will you marry me" card built online and delivered over the internet instead of handed over on paper. It carries both names, usually a photo, a written message, and in most builders a Yes button.

That category is broader than it looks. The same three words cover a printable template you buy and email as a PDF, an animated [e-card](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-card) that loops inside a chat window, and a full single-page website with its own URL. The third has no settled name yet, which is a large part of why nobody explains how it differs from the first.

Worth separating early: "proposal card" also means a *bridesmaid* proposal card. Search the phrase and roughly half of what comes back is wedding-party stationery rather than a marriage proposal. This post is about the other one.

## The three formats, and what each one can actually do

Each format below is described the same way: what it is, who it suits, what it costs, and how long it takes.

### 1. A static image you download and send

A JPG, PNG or PDF you personalise in a design tool and export. It suits anyone proposing in person who wants something to hold up on a screen or print at a photo shop. Free on most template sites, and 10–20 minutes of work, most of it spent choosing a design. It cannot react to being opened and it cannot tell you whether it was — but nothing about it can break, and that is not a small thing.

### 2. An animated file — GIF or short video

The same card with motion, exported as a GIF or MP4 and sent through WhatsApp or Instagram. It suits someone who wants a little theatre but is sending through a chat app where a bare link preview looks flat. Usually free, sometimes watermarked, and 15–30 minutes to make. It autoplays inside the conversation, which is its real advantage over a link, and it still cannot take an answer.

### 3. A hosted link that opens into a page

A URL that opens a page built for one person: their name, your photographs, a song that starts on tap, a countdown, a Yes button that logs the reply. It suits long-distance proposals and anyone who wants the asking itself to be the event. Free to build on most builders. On SubhSandesh the median gap between a page's first save and its last edit is 6.3 hours — that figure is sampled on the "I love you" template, n=1,136, not on proposals — which says people start these, walk away, and come back to them.

## Which format fits which moment

The table compares the three formats on the things that actually differ, with one column drawn from SubhSandesh's own page data.

| Format | What it can hold | Survives a screenshot | Readable in five years | SubhSandesh data |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Static image (JPG/PDF) | Names, photo, written message | Yes, it already is one | Yes — a file on their phone | Not applicable; files are not hosted |
| Animated GIF or video | Motion, no reliable sound | One frame of it | Yes, if they saved it | Not applicable; files are not hosted |
| Hosted link | Song, countdown, Yes button, password lock | No | Only while the host stays live | 40.0% of 4,524 pages are password-locked before sharing, platform-wide |
| Link plus a saved screenshot | Both, at the cost of one extra step | Yes | Yes | 48.9% of 51,164 views are on a phone, where a screenshot is one gesture |

The bottom row is the honest recommendation. Send the link for the moment, then screenshot the page yourself and send that too, so the keepsake does not depend on anyone's hosting bill.

## What a link can do that a file cannot, and what it costs you

Four things, none of which a JPG can imitate: audio that starts when they tap, a countdown that changes every time the page is reloaded, a Yes button whose answer reaches you, and a password so the page cannot be opened by whoever picks up the phone first. On SubhSandesh, 92.9% of started pages are actually published and shared — 4,204 of 4,524 — which suggests the format is not the thing people abandon.

The cost is dependence. A file is finished the moment it is exported; a link is a promise that a server, a domain renewal and a company will all still exist when it is next opened. The Pew Research Center's [May 2024 study of link rot](https://www.pewresearch.org/data-labs/2024/05/17/when-online-content-disappears/) found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were gone a decade later, and that of all pages sampled between 2013 and 2023, 9% were unreachable because the entire root domain had stopped working. Not the page — the whole site.

That is the inconvenient part, and most card builders will not print it next to their Create button.

## Will the card still be there in ten years?

Probably not, if it is only a link, and the research on why is older than the problem. A 2006 field study of personal digital archiving by Catherine Marshall and colleagues, [posted openly on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/0704.3653), found that experienced home computer users had already lost irreplaceable digital material — photos, creative work, records — while holding strong beliefs about "the incorruptibility of digital forms". People assume digital means permanent. It does not.

The counterweight is that digital things do get kept when they feel like possessions. A 2025 Frontiers in Psychology study of 294 university students found [emotional attachment was a significant predictor of digital photo hoarding](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1607274/full) — people do not delete images tied to someone they care about, even when they never look at them again. A screenshot of a proposal page is exactly that kind of image.

Peer-reviewed work comparing physical and digital keepsakes points the same way. Petrelli and Whittaker's fieldwork on [family mementos in the home](https://shura.shu.ac.uk/2907/), published in *Personal and Ubiquitous Computing* in 2010, reported that physical mementos were highly valued and varied, while digital ones were seen as less valuable, narrower in form and rarely accessed. A link is the least material object in that spectrum. A saved image is at least a thing.

## How to send it so it actually lands

Send it on WhatsApp or Instagram, not email, and expect it to be opened on a phone: 48.9% of SubhSandesh views are on phones, and 49.1% on a touch device of some kind. Design accordingly — a page that only works landscape on a laptop has already lost.

Turn the password on if there is any chance someone else holds the phone. Two in five SubhSandesh creators do, across every template, which is a strong hint about how private people consider these pages to be.

Send it when they can look at it properly. There is no first-party lead-time data for proposals, so the useful rule is a boring one: not during work, not while they are driving, not in a group chat.

And the channel is part of the message rather than a delivery detail. A 2025 study of messenger-based gifting across Korea, Japan and China, [interviewing 26 university students](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.16932), concluded that the choice of gifting platform is "not merely logistical but a culturally meaningful part of the gifting process" — and reported that senders deliberately avoid casual digital channels for emotionally significant moments. A proposal is the most emotionally significant one there is.

If you want the link version, SubhSandesh's [Will You Marry Me proposal page](https://subhsandesh.in/proposal) is a scrapbook of your story ending in a Yes button that grows every time they dodge it. For the free-tool comparison and the exact steps, see the sibling posts on [making a digital proposal card for a girlfriend online free](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/digital-proposal-card-for-girlfriend-online-free) and on [Propose Day greeting cards online free](https://subhsandesh.in/blog/propose-day-greeting-card-online-free).

## When a virtual proposal card is the wrong choice

When you are in the same room. A card on a screen in a restaurant is a worse object than a card on paper, and no amount of animation fixes that.

When the answer is genuinely uncertain. A page that logs a Yes is a lovely record of a Yes and a cruel record of anything else. Ask in person; send the card afterwards.

When what you actually want is not a question. If the impulse is "send her flowers", a proposal card is the wrong shape entirely — SubhSandesh's [build-a-bouquet page](https://subhsandesh.in/bouquet-gf) is the third most-created template on the platform at 1,094 pages, 24.2% of everything made, precisely because sending something is a different act from asking something. And if the question is "will you be my girlfriend" rather than "will you marry me", SubhSandesh's "I love you" page is the honest fit — the most-created template on the platform at 1,136 pages, carrying 16,345 views, 31.9% of all views.

Finally, when the recipient has no smartphone, or patchy data. A link needs a connection; an image does not.

## Sources

- Pew Research Center, "When Online Content Disappears", 17 May 2024 — link rot rates.
- Yu and Chang, *Frontiers in Psychology*, 15 September 2025 — digital photo hoarding, n=294.
- Lee et al., "Understanding Digital Gifting Through Messengers Across Cultures", arXiv, 21 September 2025 — 26 interviews.
- Petrelli and Whittaker, "Family memories in the home", *Personal and Ubiquitous Computing*, 2010 — physical versus digital mementos.
- Marshall, Bly and Brun-Cottan, "The Long Term Fate of Our Digital Belongings", IS&T Archiving 2006 — lost personal digital material.

auditReport.honestAssessment: An answer engine asked 'image or link for a proposal card?' has, today, no page that answers it — the SERP is Etsy printables, bridesmaid stationery and builders that show a Create button without naming what the format costs you. This post is the only one pairing the file-versus-link distinction with a measured link-rot rate and with password, phone and edit-time behaviour nobody else can publish. Structural limitation, stated plainly: no proposal-specific first-party figure was obtainable for this batch — the production-read probe of the proposalpages collection was blocked — so 40.0%, 48.9%, 92.9% and 51,164 are platform-wide across all 4,524 pages and 6.3 hours is sampled on /love-gf, and the post says so in body prose every time it cites them. A per-template proposal password rate would materially strengthen the post; it closes only when that collection can be queried. On the other side, subhsandesh.in has 46 live proposal pages and ranked in none of the 11 SERPs measured for this cluster, so assume no domain authority on this query — Canva and Paperless Post outrank it on links alone and that takes months to shift, if it shifts.
